newsitem.title: CUBA: Australian, 22, to try Cuba-to-Florida swim again. [CORRECTED 22:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Australian, 22, to try Cuba-to-Florida swim again. [CORRECTED 22:35 GMT]

text.p: Attempting what no one has yet accomplished, Australian marathon swimmer Susie Maroney, 22, dived off Havana's Malecon seawall on Sunday on a second attempt to reach the shores of Florida.
The Straits of Florida are considered one of swimming's last great challenges. Success will require extraordinary stamina, indomitable will and luck.

The distance between Havana, Cuba, and Key West, Florida, is 90 miles (145 km), but Maroney said she might have to swim as much as 125 miles (200 km) in about 45 hours because of strong Gulf Stream currents.

She will follow a zigzag course to allow her to use the currents to her own advantage whenever possible. Her helpers will use satellite photos to plot the best route. A navigation expert, Ean McDonald of Australia, will sail ahead to make on-the-spot determinations and drop lighted buoys.

Maroney will avoid marauding sharks by swimming inside a big, floating cage pulled by a boat. Witnesses will watch her day and night to assure that none of the ground rules for ocean-going marathon swims are violated.
Two television crews, from Australia and the United States, will be aboard accompanying boats, filming the whole attempt.

Maroney's swim began in a breeze-ruffled, slightly undulating sea, under a somewhat overcast sky. It is Cuba's rainy season, and experts say the seas and weather in the Straits of Florida can change from hour to hour.

The Gulf Stream currents will favour Maroney during the first part of her swim. As she gets close to her goal, however, the same currents will rip eastward around the tip of Florida, forcing her to fight against their powerful tow.

A storm, heavy seas and currents forced Maroney to abandon her first attempt to swim the Straits of Florida last June when she was only 12 miles (19 km) short of the Florida Keys and after she had battled for 38-1/2 hours (corrects the conversion of 12 miles from 7.4 km to 19 km). She vomited and hallucinated before being plucked from the water.

In one attempt to swim the straits, an American was forced to give up about 12 miles (19 km) off the Cuban shore after small jellyfish and Portuguese men-of-war slipped into his shark cage and stung his face and body.

Maroney said last week while waiting in Havana for favourable weather that her crew on the accompanying boats would play music and feed her hot coffee, chocolate and baby food during her resting periods. On her abortive swim last year, she lost 24 pounds (11 kg).
The Australian swimmer has been training six hours a day for nearly a year. Echoing a famous phrase applied to Mt. Everest, she said: "The challenge is still there. ... I have to keep trying."
